notes: \cpara{Opens with history. Both quotations match the editions the post cites. Procopius wrote this in his account of the Nika riot of 532 in Constantinople (\textsc{History of the Wars}, Book I, chapter 24); Gibbon's sentence is from chapter 40 of \textsc{The Decline and Fall}.}

\cpara{The answer has support in the post's own source. In the same passage Procopius says the partisans fight ``for the sake of these names and the seats which the rival factions occupy in watching the games.'' It is also one side of a debate. Historians disagree about how far the factions, which began as racing clubs, had become political and religious parties by the sixth century; Wikipedia's article on them names Alan Cameron as representative of one side and Gavro Manojlovi\'c of the other. Gibbon's next sentence, which the post does not quote, reads: ``A secret attachment to the family or sect of Anastasius was imputed to the greens; the blues were zealously devoted to the cause of orthodoxy and Justinian.''}
\cpara{Sets up the fable: an underground society whose two factions began in a dispute over what one written word, ``cerulean,'' means, a question none of them can check.}
\cpara{Describes the truce: violence has given way to law, a middle class and schooling about the old wars, and to the idea that ``people are people, whether they be Blue or Green.''}

\cpara{Lists each faction's package of positions. The package mixes questions of value (which tax, how easy divorce should be) with questions of fact (the shape of the Earth, what it circles), and on the two questions of cosmology each side is right once. The discovery at the surface can settle only the questions of fact.}
\cpara{Describes the uneasy peace: Greens shop at Blue shops, Blues drink in Green taverns, and tolerance, even friendship, is growing.}
\cpara{The discovery. The person who walks up the corridor is given no name and no pronoun, so that the story can let each member of the party be the one.}
\cpara{Announces six branches, one for each member of the party.}
\cpara{The first branch: a Blue who takes the sky as a weapon against the Greens and ends the truce.}
\cpara{The second: a Green who reads the fact as the universe taking the Blues' side, and concludes that it ``had always been a place of evil.''}

\cpara{The third: a Blue professor who taught that the two views were ``equally valid'' and now decides to block the passage, fearing the fact will be ``misinterpreted.'' The fable here separates tolerance of people, which its earlier paragraphs welcome, from treating a question of fact as a matter of viewpoint. The first branch shows the danger Charles fears: there the discovery ends the truce.}

\cpara{The fourth: a Green who accepts the fact at great cost and becomes Blue. She is the only partisan who changes her mind, and she does it in grief: she says ``I was wrong'' to herself ``mournfully.''}

\cpara{The fifth: a Green who sees the whole history as folly over ``one pointless thing'' with ``No poetry, no beauty,'' and wonders whether everyone deserves what is coming. The next branch answers him.}

\cpara{The last branch, and the only one that ends in delight. Ferris is the only member of the party given no faction and no pronoun. The fable states no moral, but in the book ``The Meditation on Curiosity'' says that ``Ferris, the last character, embodies the power of innocent curiosity.'' The model response is thus given to the one character with no side to lose; the fable does not show how a partisan could reach it.}
\cpara{Cites the translation of Procopius quoted above.}
\cpara{Cites the volume of Gibbon quoted above.}
